title: Two Russian Psalm Settings
program_note:
Two Russian Psalm Settings was commissioned by the international music competition St. Petersburg in the Mirror of the World’s Cultural Heritage, as the required contemporary composition for the piano accompaniment competition.  The texts are both in Russian.
By the Rivers of Babylon is a setting of the first line of Psalm 137, based upon a 16th-century (or earlier) Russian Orthodox chant in an old Russian dialect.  In contrast to the restrained vocal line, the piano part is meant to bring out the emotional content of the text, with in-the-piano techniques used to evoke anguished sobs and falling tears (with a hidden reference to Bach’s An Wasserflüssen Babylon).  Happy is the Man that Fears the Lord is a setting of all of Psalm 112, based upon the traditional Russian Orthodox ‘intoning’ (or ‘reciting’) practice, whereby a cantor sings each line of text on a single tone, with a cadential formula at the end of each line.  The choir then responds with a cadential formula of its own.  Here, the piano provides the responses, but not always in the same ways.  Additionally, the piano provides reflections of the joy, fear, and anger of the text.

David S. Lefkowitz
6 March 2016
Los Angeles, CA
